newsitem.title: UK: Yeast cell gene map advances cause of science.
newsitem.headline: Yeast cell gene map advances cause of science.

text.p: Scientists said on Wednesday they had found every single gene in a yeast cell in what they described as a significant achievement that can help advance medicine and genetics.
The one-celled brewer's yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisae, is the closest relative to humans to have its genes all counted and accounted for. The others are bacteria.

"This achievement is the result of a tremendous effort, in which over 600 scientists from 96 laboratories participated in a worldwide programme...over a period of several years," Rebecca Clayton and colleagues at The Institute for Genomic Research in Rockville, Maryland, wrote in a commentary in the science journal Nature.
The map of the collection of yeast genes, which are known as a genome, is published with this week's Nature.
It is significant in that it represents a eukaryote - an organism whose cell or cells have a nucleus. This domain includes humans and other animals, plants, yeast, some fungi and slime moulds.
"The yeast genome will be used as the reference genome for all eukaryotes, including humans," Clayton's group wrote.

There will be many genes that yeast and people have in common, Clayton said in a telephone interview. This can be a useful reference for geneticists looking for ways to treat genetic disease, for instance.
"Physiologically yeast does a lot of the same things that human cells do," she said.

"Some of the basic physiological processes would be there. We certainly share some cell division similarities (and) how we derive energy from things like sugar. Basic energy needs are very similar across all cellular organisms."
While humans have about 80,000 genes -- this genome is still being mapped -- the yeast has 6,000, Clayton said. About a third of these have no known function.
"These 'orphan' genes are a vast virgin territory to geneticists and protein chemists," they wrote.
"It's like discovering an unknown continent," Clayton added.
"Is there a core set of genes for all organisms? Can any organism be considered a 'model' system?" they asked in the commentary.
